description: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. Her question is framed as an issue of individual choice inviting the response: “Not me if I can avoid it.” The responsible answer is, of course, all of us – collectively. description: Poet and writer whose collection Elegies channelled grief into exquisite poetry and won the Whitbread book of the year Douglas Dunn, who has died aged 83, was overjoyed to find himself among the poetic aristocracy at Faber and Faber in 1969. His first book, Terry Street, had been accepted “by the publisher which issued Eliot, Pound, Auden, Larkin, Ted Hughes, Thom Gunn, and Seamus Heaney . When my copies arrived, I kissed them.” Dunn stuck with Faber throughout his writing life, and they with him. The successful quartet of Heaney , Hughes , Larkin and Gunn – following on from the Eliot-led ensemble of the 1920s and 30s – might have become a quintet, but Dunn’s leftwing commitment and his adherence to rigorous prosody set him apart from the hedonism of Gunn, on the one hand, and the likable populism of Heaney, on the other.

description: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment Back in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”. The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them.
